source.title: Broken neural scaling laws in materials science
source.authors: Max Großmann; M. Grunert; Erich Runge

record.file_problem: Whole paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling curves in materials-science GNNs and reports broken dataset-size scaling and saturating parameter scaling, challenging the generalization that the same power-law form holds beyond text pretraining. It does not test the original language-model setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own scaling measurements for materials-science prediction, not language-model pretraining. It also compares architecture variants. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows. It does not test small-run extrapolation or a compute-budget-optimal parameter/token split.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own scaling curves of validation loss against dataset size and parameter count, separately and jointly, for materials-science GNNs predicting dielectric functions. These results bear on V5 (whether the power-law form holds outside text pretraining) and on V7 (curves bending away from a single power law, and exponents depending on setup and fit choices). This is a new setting with a result on the claim, so T3 fits better than the reader's T5: the data does not show the power-law trend absent, it shows a qualified form. There are no language models, so V1–V4 and V6 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. Add that broken data scaling persists when D and N vary jointly, and that simple power-law scaling appears only when data and capacity are well matched. Message-passing type has little effect on scaling, while three-body interactions improve data scaling but not parameter scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales materials-science invariant GNNs against dataset size and parameter count using a composite MAE validation loss, rather than measuring language-model held-out cross-entropy across parameters, tokens, and training compute. It does not measure compute-optimal allocation or test extrapolation from small runs.
record.method_sensitivity: Data-scaling behavior changes with model capacity in the 2D analysis; data exponents differ between OptiMetal2B and OptiMetal3B. The authors report little influence of CGC versus TC message passing on scaling trends. Architecture comparisons also show differing effects for pooling, node embedding, and message passing.

fits_no_version.finding: In GNNs at roughly fixed N (~7–8M), swapping individual components changes validation loss by up to ~5% (pooling 1.068→1.126). Varying the Spectra-MLP width multiplier changes loss only through parameter count (Supp. Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In materials GNNs, component choice (pooling, embedding) matters more than width allocation at fixed parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal maximum learning rate falls as a power law in N; the authors adopted ηmax ∝ N^-1 for TC models (Supp. Note 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rate scales as a power of parameter count in materials GNNs.

record.problems: The scaling study concerns one materials-science prediction task and two invariant GNN architectures. Scaling losses are validation losses, not held-out test losses. Each fit averages three random initializations. The study does not report out-of-range extrapolation tests, a compute-optimal allocation, or language-model results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported scaling or architecture comparison was omitted.

untested.parts: No language models or LM pretraining loss.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
No compute budget or compute-optimal allocation.
No LM depth/width-at-fixed-N test; only GNN component swaps.
Only one materials-science regression task; no image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No LM parameter-counting conventions, training schedules or compute-optimal splits; no comparison of published laws.

missing.what: In the 2D maps, data scaling saturates around D=40k for the smallest models, is a simple power law at N≈1M, and becomes broken again for overparameterized models. This is reported qualitatively, with no per-N exponents.
AICc comparison of the four 1D forms. For OptiMetal2B (TC) parameter scaling, the broken power law with amplitude beats the adopted saturation-floor form (−56.10 vs −54.73).
AICc for the joint fits: the Kaplan-type form beats the Hoffmann additive form (−344.50 vs −253.68 for 2B; −359.55 vs −285.21 for 3B).

record.verdict_notes: V4 labels are removed: rows r9–r11 are architecture-optimization selection values for GNN component swaps, not LM shape tests. The reader's 'challenges' on V5 is downgraded to limits_scope, because loss still falls with D in power-law segments; only the single-exponent form fails. Table II in the extracted text is garbled, so the Dc and N0 values in r7 and r8 need checking against the PDF.

versions.untested_parts: No language models, held-out language-model pretraining loss, or sweeps over language-model parameters, tokens, and compute.
No test of whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Dataset size and parameter count are varied, but no compute budget or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is measured.
Architecture comparisons concern invariant materials GNNs, not language models; the study does not test depth and width across a broad language-model architecture range.
Tests scaling in materials-science prediction, not image/video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, transfer, or other listed regimes.
No downstream-task performance is evaluated as a function of pretraining loss or scale.

The study reports curve bending and dependence on model capacity and body order in materials GNNs. It does not test language-model parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or compute-optimal splits, and does not establish that published language-model laws disagree because of fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Parameter scaling and joint D–N fits in invariant materials GNNs
relationships.reason: Loss falls as a power law in N (αN 0.41–0.58) up to a saturation floor at fixed D. A Kaplan-type joint form fits far better than the additive form (r4–r8).
relationships.display_finding: Loss follows parameter power laws with exponents 0.41–0.58 before saturating at fixed data size, and a Kaplan-type joint form fits substantially better than the additive form.

relation.reason: The study measures and compares scaling forms using its own materials-GNN validation losses, directly testing V5 and V7.

tranche.reason: The central result requires qualifying the single-power-law extension in V5: broken data scaling persists when data and capacity vary jointly. This meets T5 beyond merely introducing a new setting.

source_check.notes: Supplementary Note 7 calls the better OptiMetal2B (TC) parameter fit amplitude-bearing, but Table IX assigns −56.10 to the broken law without amplitude, −44.71 with amplitude, and −54.73 to the adopted saturation-floor fit. Reported standard deviations concern validation-loss points across initializations; the fit tables do not report exponent uncertainties.

statements.correction: Materials-GNN data scaling: smoothly broken power laws; steeper high-data exponents; simple data scaling at intermediate capacity; V5 label=limits_scope.
statements.problem: The description of this study's broken data curves is correct, but the challenges label overstates its implication: power-law improvement remains present in individual regimes.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: All three 1D data-scaling fits are broken power laws, with a reported change from a low-data to a steeper high-data exponent rather than one simple power law (r1–r3).
